title: Signature Choosing the Right Channel
body:
The Signature Channel Ladder is an original Signature design that ranks channels by how much of a conversation they preserve. Email sits at the top of the ladder because it keeps words, attachments, and dates together in one place. A call sits in the middle because it carries tone but keeps nothing unless someone writes it down, and a short message sits at the base because it is fast and forgettable by design. The ladder tells the sender to climb only as high as the decision deserves.

Method. To use the ladder, name the decision first and find its rung: a record-worthy decision climbs to email, a tone-sensitive decision stops at a call, and a passing coordination note stays at the base as a short message. Every climb ends with a written landing, a short summary sent to everyone involved, so the conversation's height is never lost when the call ends.

Checklist.

  • Name the decision before choosing a channel
  • Find its rung on the Signature ladder
  • Climb only as high as the decision deserves
  • Land every call with a written summary
  • Keep the summary with the original thread

Use and limits. The Signature ladder is a design for choosing channels, not a claim that any existing tool works this way, and it does not override an organisation's own communication rules. title: Signature Writing a Clear Email
body:
The Signature Subject Seal is an original Signature design in which every email subject carries three marks in order: the topic, the action, and the date it matters by. A sealed subject can be understood without opening the message, and a reader scanning a crowded inbox can sort sealed mail by action instead of by sender. The seal is a discipline for the writer, not a feature of any mail program.

Method. To seal a subject, write the topic in two to four words, add the action verb the reader must take, and add the date the action matters by. Then write the body to match the seal exactly: if the seal promises a decision by Friday, the body must contain the decision and the Friday date, or the seal is broken and the reader learns not to trust it.

Checklist.

  • Topic in two to four words
  • Action verb the reader must take
  • Date the action matters by
  • Body matches the seal exactly
  • A broken seal is fixed, not ignored

title: Signature The Useful Reply
body:
The Signature Answer Ledger is an original Signature design that treats every incoming message as a small ledger of questions owed. Each question becomes a line, each answer closes its line, and the ledger stays open until every line is closed or honestly deferred with a date. A reply sent from a ledger can never silently drop a question, because the open lines are visible to the writer before sending.

Method. To keep a ledger, copy each question from the incoming message as its own line, write the answer beside it, and leave deferred lines open with a promised date. Send the reply only when no line is open without a date, and carry deferred lines forward into the next message so they are never lost between threads.

Checklist.

  • Copy each question as a ledger line
  • Answer beside its line
  • Defer only with a promised date
  • Send only when no line is dateless
  • Carry deferred lines into the next reply

title: Signature Group Messages Done Well
body:
The Signature Circle Rule is an original Signature design for group messages: a circle holds at most the people a decision truly needs, and every circle carries its purpose in its name. When a new person is needed, the circle grows by announcement, with the purpose restated, so no one wakes up inside a conversation they do not understand. When the purpose ends, the circle closes with a summary, not by silent drift.

Method. To apply the rule, write the purpose before inviting anyone, invite only the people the purpose names, and restate the purpose whenever the circle grows. Keep decisions inside the circle's thread, and close the circle with a final summary that names what was decided and what remains open.

Checklist.

  • Write the purpose before inviting anyone
  • Invite only the people the purpose names
  • Restate the purpose when the circle grows
  • Keep decisions in the circle thread
  • Close with a final summary

title: Signature Tone in Text
body:
The Signature Tone Frame is an original Signature design that wraps every sensitive message in three visible parts: a greeting that names the relationship, a body that states the content plainly, and a close that states the writer's intent. The frame does not change the content, it changes how the content arrives, so a reader never has to guess whether a short message is busy, angry, or simply brief.

Method. To frame a message, open with a greeting, write the content without sarcasm or coded language, and close by naming the intent, such as asking, informing, or deciding. If the content is criticism, the frame carries it as a request for change rather than a judgement of character, which keeps the conversation repairable.

Checklist.

  • Greeting names the relationship
  • Body states content plainly
  • Close states the writer's intent
  • Criticism arrives as a request for change
  • No sarcasm in framed messages

title: Signature Voice Notes With Care
body:
The Signature Voice Ribbon is an original Signature design that pairs every voice note with a short text ribbon: the point in one line, plus any facts the listener will need again. The ribbon lets the listener decide when to listen and lets them find the facts later without replaying the audio. A voice note without a ribbon is treated as unfinished, however warm it sounds.

Method. To tie a ribbon, write one line stating the point, list any dates, names, or numbers from the note, and send the ribbon with the audio, not after it. If the note contains no facts, the ribbon simply says what the note is about, so the listener can choose the right moment to hear it.

Checklist.

  • One line stating the point
  • Facts listed in text
  • Ribbon sent with the audio
  • No ribbon means unfinished
  • Listener chooses when to listen

title: Signature Setting Up a Video Call
body:
The Signature Call Door is an original Signature design that treats a video call as a door with a sign on it: the sign carries the link, the time, the purpose, and the fallback contact, all in one place. A guest who finds the door can enter without asking the host for directions, and a guest who finds the door locked knows exactly whom to contact. The design removes the hunt for details across scattered messages.

Method. To hang a door, write one message containing link, time with time zone, purpose, and fallback contact, and send it early enough for the guest to test it. Test your own camera and microphone from the guest's side where possible, and join early so the first person through the door finds a host, not an empty room.

Checklist.

  • One message holds link, time, purpose, fallback
  • Sent early enough to test
  • Host tests from the guest side
  • Host joins early
  • Locked door names whom to contact

title: Signature Looking and Sounding Good on Video
body:
The Signature Stage Check is an original Signature design that treats the caller's space as a small stage checked before every performance. The check walks three points in order: light, sound, and background, and the caller does not join until all three pass. A failed point is fixed before the call, never explained away during it, so the audience's attention stays on the conversation instead of the staging.

Method. To run the stage check, stand where you will sit and look at your own preview: light on your face, camera at eye level, background clear of private items. Speak one test sentence and listen for echo or noise, then mute until the call begins. Record the check as done, so a repeated failure in the same spot gets fixed at its source rather than endured at every call.

Checklist.

  • Light on face in preview
  • Camera at eye level
  • Background clear of private items
  • Test sentence without echo
  • Mute until the call begins

title: Signature Running a Small Video Meeting
body:
The Signature Meeting Compass is an original Signature design that gives every small meeting four points: purpose, items, decisions, and owners. The compass is drawn before the meeting and filled during it, so the meeting can never drift without the drift being visible: an item with no decision is an open point on the compass, and an ownerless decision is a direction no one is walking. The compass is closed only when every point is filled or honestly carried forward.

Method. To use the compass, write the purpose at the centre and the items around it, each with a time. During the meeting, record each decision beside its item and name its owner before moving on. At the close, read the compass aloud, and carry any open point into the next meeting's centre so it is never lost.

Checklist.

  • Purpose at the centre
  • Items around it with times
  • Decision beside each item
  • Owner named before moving on
  • Open points carried to the next compass

title: Signature The Follow-Up Summary
body:
The Signature Landing Note is an original Signature design that ends every call with a short note landing in the same place the call began. The note carries only three things: decisions, owners, and dates, in that order, and it is sent before the participants scatter to other work. A call without a landing note is treated as a conversation that has not yet landed, however pleasant it felt.

Method. To write a landing note, list each decision in the order it was made, name the owner of each next step, and give each step a date. Send the note to all participants and invite corrections within one working day. If a correction arrives, the note is revised and resent, so the landed version is always the corrected version.

Checklist.

  • Decisions in the order made
  • Owner for each next step
  • Date for each step
  • Sent before participants scatter
  • Corrections revised and resent

title: Signature Response-Time Boundaries
body:
The Signature Quiet Hours Charter is an original Signature design in which each person publishes simple quiet hours and a single urgent route. Contacts read the charter before messaging, so a message sent during quiet hours is understood as waiting, not ignored, and a message sent through the urgent route is understood as genuinely urgent. The charter replaces guessing with reading.

Method. To write a charter, name your quiet hours, name your normal reply window, and name the one route for genuinely urgent matters, such as a call. Share the charter with regular contacts and keep it where they can find it, and honour other people's charters by waiting during their quiet hours unless the matter truly belongs on the urgent route.

Checklist.

  • Quiet hours named
  • Normal reply window named
  • One urgent route named
  • Charter shared with regular contacts
  • Others' charters honoured

title: Signature Communicating Across Time Zones
body:
The Signature Two-Clocks Rule is an original Signature design that requires every cross-zone message to carry two clocks: the sender's time and the reader's time, side by side. A message that says only one clock asks the reader to do the conversion and invites the error; a message that carries both clocks lets the reader check the conversion at a glance. Deadlines under the rule carry the judging zone in bold words, never hidden in an abbreviation.

Method. To apply the rule, convert the time before writing, write both clocks in the message, and name the judging zone for every deadline in full words. When proposing meetings, propose from the other side's working hours outward, and rotate the inconvenient slot across the group so the same side does not always rise early or stay late.

Checklist.

  • Sender's clock and reader's clock side by side
  • Convert before writing, not after
  • Judging zone named in full words
  • Propose from the other side's hours
  • Rotate the inconvenient slot

title: Signature Accessible Everyday Communication
body:
The Signature Open Door Format is an original Signature design in which every important message arrives in two forms at once: the form it was made in, and a plain-text form that carries the same facts. A call arrives with its summary, a voice note arrives with its ribbon, an image arrives with its description, so no one is locked out by the form a message happens to take. The format is a habit of sending, not a property of any tool.

Method. To use the format, send the plain-text companion with the original, never hours later, and make the companion complete on its own, so a reader of the companion alone still learns the facts. Check the companion against the original before sending, and invite corrections from anyone it does not serve, treating each correction as a fix to the format rather than a complaint about it.

Checklist.

  • Original and plain-text companion together
  • Companion sent at the same time
  • Companion complete on its own
  • Companion checked against the original
  • Corrections treated as format fixes

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Signature Accessible Everyday Communication. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: forms sent: 2; companion present: True; open door: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The Signature open door format is a practice design, not a feature of any existing messaging program, and it does not replace professional accessibility services where those are needed. It governs everyday messages, where a companion text is often the difference between inclusion and exclusion. title: Signature Correcting a Mis-Sent Message
body:
The Signature Clean Correction is an original Signature design that repairs a mis-sent message with a fixed three-line form: the error named, the correction given, and the apology offered, in that order, with nothing else added. The form's strictness is its kindness: the reader finds the correction at once, the wrong version is clearly marked as wrong, and the apology does not bury either under explanation.

Method. To make a clean correction, write the three lines in order, send them in the same channel as the error, and mark the original as superseded where the channel allows it. Then check with the affected people that they hold the corrected version, and record the correction alongside the original so later readers meet the correction first.

Checklist.

  • Error named first
  • Correction given second
  • Apology offered third
  • Original marked as superseded
  • Correction travels with the original

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Signature Correcting a Mis-Sent Message. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: correction lines: 3; form complete: True; first line: error named Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The Signature clean correction is a writing discipline, not a feature of any existing messaging program, and it cannot recall messages already forwarded or copied. It governs what the sender does next, which is the part that limits how far an error travels. title: Signature Keeping a Record of Decisions
body:
The Signature Decision Ledger is an original Signature design that keeps every decision as a ledger entry with five fields: decision, date, owners, thread pointer, and status. Entries are never edited in place; a changed decision becomes a new entry that supersedes the old one, so the history of a decision stays readable instead of being rewritten. The ledger is the memory of the group, kept where the group can read it.

Method. To keep the ledger, add an entry for each decision on the day it is made, fill all five fields, and mark superseded entries rather than deleting them. Search the ledger before making a related decision, and review the ledger at natural pauses, such as the end of a project phase, to close entries whose work is done.

Checklist.

  • Five fields per entry
  • New entry supersedes, never overwrites
  • Superseded entries marked, not deleted
  • Search before related decisions
  • Review and close finished entries

Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. The Signature decision ledger is a practice design, not a feature of any existing messaging program, and it does not replace formal record-keeping where an organisation or the law requires it. It governs everyday decisions, where a small findable note prevents most repeated arguments. title: Signature Checking Before Acting on an Urgent Request
body:
The Signature Second Door is an original Signature design that requires every urgent request to pass through two doors before action: the door it arrived through, and a second door the requester did not choose, such as a known number or an in-person word. A request that passes both doors is treated as genuine; a request that passes only the first is treated as waiting, however urgent its wording. The second door is chosen in advance, during calm, not improvised during urgency.

Method. To set a second door, agree with regular contacts in advance how urgent requests will be confirmed, such as a call to a known number or a code word spoken in person. When an urgent request arrives, open the second door before acting, and record the confirmation with the action so the verification can be shown later. If the second door cannot be opened, the request waits, and waiting is treated as the safe outcome rather than a failure.

Checklist.

  • Second door chosen in advance
  • Request must pass both doors
  • Confirmation recorded with the action
  • Unconfirmed requests wait
  • Waiting treated as the safe outcome

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Signature Checking Before Acting on an Urgent Request. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: doors passed: 1 of 2; act now: False; status: waiting Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The Signature second door is a practice design, not a security product, and it does not guarantee that a verified request is wise, only that it came from the claimed sender as far as the second door can show. Where money or credentials are involved and doubt remains, seeking independent advice is still the right step.
